analysis.investment_thesis: The Oberoi brand is one of the finest in global luxury hospitality — a genuine moat built over 75 years that commands premium pricing and high occupancy from discerning travelers. However, hotels are capital-intensive, COVID proved the business model goes deeply negative in crises, and at 26.5x earnings the stock prices in a lot of the recovery already.
key_strengths: Exceptional operating margins of 38.91% — among the highest in Indian hospitality — reflecting genuine luxury brand pricing power rather than volume-driven economics
Near debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.05, INR 250 Cr borrowings vs INR 4,706 Cr equity) gives EIH resilience through downturns that leveraged hotel chains lack
ROE has recovered to 18% and ROCE to 23.4% as hotels fill up post-COVID, demonstrating the underlying asset quality when demand normalizes
key_risks: Hotels are fundamentally capital-intensive — capex jumped from INR 67 Cr (FY22) to INR 485 Cr (FY25) as expansion accelerates, and returns on new properties take years to mature
COVID demonstrated extreme earnings fragility: net profit went from INR 165 Cr (FY20) to -INR 375 Cr (FY21) and -INR 95 Cr (FY22) — this is not a toll bridge
Promoter holding at 32.85% is relatively low for a family-heritage brand; ITC holds a large strategic stake, creating some corporate governance complexity
red_flags: Free cash flow dropped from INR 494 Cr (FY24) to INR 346 Cr (FY25) even as profits rose to INR 770 Cr — heavy capex is absorbing cash that should compound for shareholders
OCF was negative in FY21 and FY22 — only 3 of 5 years positive — a reminder that hotel revenues are highly discretionary and correlated to macro shocks
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Oberoi is a brand I deeply respect — it represents genuine craftsmanship and commands prices that competitors simply cannot match. The 38.9% operating margin in FY25 proves the pricing power is real. A nearly debt-free balance sheet for a hotel company is unusual and admirable discipline. These are qualities worth owning.

My hesitation is twofold. First, hotels require continuous reinvestment — you must maintain the physical product to maintain the brand, and EIH's capex is accelerating sharply (INR 485 Cr in FY25 vs. INR 222 Cr in FY24). Second, at 26.5x earnings, the market is pricing in sustained luxury travel growth with no disruptions. COVID reminded us that even the finest brand cannot fill rooms during a global shutdown. At a more compelling price — say 18-20x — this would be a clear buy. Today it is a hold for those who own it.
